checks.prompt: Two engineers argue about which audio library to use. One is exploring beat, chroma and pitch features over a music collection on a laptop; the other is feeding spectrograms into a neural network trained on an accelerator, with on-the-fly augmentation. Who should use which, and what is the actual difference between them?
checks.explanation: The two libraries implement the same pipeline — frame, window, transform, power, perceptual warping, logarithm — but for different jobs. One is an eager array toolkit returning ordinary arrays at every step, with the richest music-information-retrieval toolbox, ideal for analysis and prototyping. The other expresses the same transforms as modules inside a computation graph: batched, accelerator-ready and differentiable, which is what makes augmentation and learnable front ends part of the model rather than a preprocessing step. Most real projects use both — one to explore, the other in the training loop.
options: They compute the same signal processing but live in different worlds. The eager array-based toolkit suits the first: everything returns plain arrays, it has the richest set of music-analysis features, and it is the least ceremony for exploration on a processor. The framework-native library suits the second: the same transforms expressed as composable modules that are batched, run on an accelerator and are differentiable, so an augmentation mask or a learnable front end is simply part of the model
One is for music and the other for speech; the underlying transforms differ, so their outputs are not comparable in principle
The framework-native one is strictly better and the array-based one is deprecated; the only reason to use the latter is legacy code
They are interchangeable wrappers around the same backend, so the choice is purely stylistic

checks.prompt: Describe the single pipeline both libraries compute, naming each stage and the parameter that controls it. Then state the loading contract that differs between them — three properties for each — and explain concretely what goes wrong downstream when that difference is overlooked.
checks.expected: A correct answer must walk one path: the waveform is cut into overlapping frames and windowed, controlled by the transform size and the hop between frames; each frame is transformed to the frequency domain, giving one more than half the transform size in frequency bins; magnitudes are squared to power; a perceptual filterbank collapses those bins into a smaller number of bands, controlled by the band count and the frequency limits; and finally a logarithm, or a further decorrelating transform, produces the feature. The contract must be given for both loaders across three properties. The eager toolkit's loader by DEFAULT resamples to a fixed rate of about twenty-two thousand samples a second, downmixes to a single channel, and returns a one-dimensional array. The framework-native loader keeps the file's own sample rate, keeps every channel, and returns a two-dimensional per-channel tensor. The downstream consequence must be concrete: everything after loading is expressed in units of the sample rate, so assuming the file's original rate after a default load makes every pitch, tempo, frame-timing and frequency-axis number wrong — silently, with no error — and code written for one shape convention breaks or misbehaves on the other. A strong answer notes that both defaults are opt-out through separate arguments, that raw integer samples must be scaled into the range minus one to one first, and that the two libraries' decorrelated cepstral features will not match numerically because their conventions differ, so a pipeline should pick one and not compare across them.

checks.prompt: A team's features look wrong in three ways: values are enormous, the loudness scale is nonsensical, and a hard-coded frame index no longer points where they expect after changing the transform size. Which explanations are right?
checks.explanation: Three separate everyday mistakes. Integer samples span tens of thousands rather than the range minus one to one that these pipelines expect, so scaling is mandatory rather than cosmetic. The decibel conversion has to match what you have: the perceptual spectrogram from one library is already power, so the power conversion is correct and applying an amplitude conversion — or converting twice — produces meaningless numbers. And frame counts are subject to edge padding and rounding, which differ between settings and between libraries, so an index that happens to be right today is fragile.
options: Enormous values mean raw integer samples were used without scaling into the range minus one to one, so every derived quantity is off by a factor of tens of thousands. The nonsensical loudness scale is a double logarithm: one library's perceptual spectrogram already returns POWER, so the power-to-decibel conversion is the right one and applying an amplitude conversion, or converting twice, gives nonsense. And frame indices should not be hard-coded because edge handling and rounding differ, so counts can shift by one between settings and libraries

Enormous values come from the wrong window function; the loudness scale is fixed by raising the band count; and frame indices are stable across all settings so the third symptom indicates a corrupted file
All three are sample-rate problems and disappear once the file is resampled to a common rate
Enormous values are expected and harmless because the logarithm removes scale; the loudness problem is the frequency limits; and frame indices depend only on the hop, so nothing can shift them

checks.prompt: Model the arithmetic and the contracts. Define `LIBROSA_DEFAULT_SR = 22050` and `INT16_SCALE = 32768`. Write `frame_count(num_samples, n_fft, hop, center=True)` raising `ValueError` for a non-positive `n_fft` or `hop`, returning `1 + num_samples // hop` when centre padding is used and otherwise 0 when the clip is shorter than one window and `1 + (num_samples - n_fft) // hop` when it is not. Write `spectrogram_shape(num_samples, n_fft, hop, center=True)` returning the pair (one more than half the transform size, the frame count). Write `normalise_pcm16(samples)` dividing each integer sample by `INT16_SCALE`, raising `ValueError` for a non-integer value (a boolean counts as non-integer) or one outside the signed 16-bit range. Write `to_channels_first(array)` returning a per-channel list of COPIES — wrapping a flat list of numbers as a single channel and copying a list of channels as it is — raising `ValueError` for empty input. Write `to_mono(array)` returning the element-wise mean across channels, or a copy of the single channel. Write `load_contract(library, native_sr, channels, sr="unset", mono="unset")` returning `{"sample_rate", "channels", "ndim"}`: for the framework-native library, the native rate, every channel and two dimensions; for the eager toolkit, the rate is the fixed default when `sr` was not supplied, the native rate when it was supplied as None, and otherwise the value given, while `mono` defaults to true — a mono result has one channel and one dimension, a non-mono result keeps the channels and has two. Raise `ValueError` for any other library name. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The frame arithmetic contains a genuinely surprising fact: with centre padding the count depends only on the hop, so two different transform sizes give the identical number of frames — and without it the window length matters and a short clip produces nothing at all. The same audio and the same parameters therefore give different counts under the two settings, which is exactly why hard-coding a frame index is fragile. The contract block at the end is the bug that catches nearly everyone. One loader hands the file back as it is; the other, by default, both resamples to a fixed rate and collapses the channels — two separate opt-out switches, neither of which announces itself. The final assertions make the damage concrete: after a default load the number of frames for a one-second clip is simply different, and every downstream quantity expressed in units of the sample rate is wrong with no error anywhere.
checks.test:
# With centre padding the frame count depends only on the hop, which is the formula
# worth remembering when sizing buffers.
assert frame_count(16_000, 512, 256) == 1 + 16_000 // 256 == 63
assert frame_count(16_000, 1024, 256) == 63, "centre padding hides n_fft"
assert frame_count(0, 512, 256) == 1

# Without it the window length matters and a short clip yields nothing at all.
assert frame_count(16_000, 512, 256, center=False) == 1 + (16_000 - 512) // 256
assert frame_count(511, 512, 256, center=False) == 0
assert frame_count(512, 512, 256, center=False) == 1
# ...so the SAME audio and the same parameters give different counts under the two
# settings, which is why hard-coding a frame index is a bug waiting to happen.
assert frame_count(16_000, 512, 256) != frame_count(16_000, 512, 256, center=False)

assert spectrogram_shape(16_000, 512, 256) == (257, 63)
assert spectrogram_shape(16_000, 1024, 256)[0] == 513
assert spectrogram_shape(16_000, 512, 128)[1] > spectrogram_shape(16_000, 512, 256)[1]
for bad in ((16_000, 512, 0), (16_000, 0, 256)):
    try:
        frame_count(*bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad} must be refused")

# Raw integer samples are not what these libraries expect: without dividing by the
# full-scale value the numbers are thousands of times too large and every feature
# derived from them is meaningless.
assert normalise_pcm16([0]) == [0.0]
assert normalise_pcm16([-32768]) == [-1.0]
assert abs(normalise_pcm16([32767])[0] - 0.999969482421875) < 1e-12
assert all(-1.0 <= v <= 1.0 for v in normalise_pcm16([-32768, -1, 0, 1, 32767]))
for bad in ([32768], [-32769], [0.5], [True]):
    try:
        normalise_pcm16(bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad} must be refused")

# The two shape conventions: one library hands back a flat mono array, the other
# always a per-channel one, so bridging is explicit rather than automatic.
assert to_channels_first([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]) == [[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]]
assert to_channels_first([[0.1, 0.2], [0.3, 0.4]]) == [[0.1, 0.2], [0.3, 0.4]]
assert to_mono([0.1, 0.2]) == [0.1, 0.2]
assert to_mono([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]]) == [0.5, 0.5]
assert to_mono([[2.0], [4.0], [6.0]]) == [4.0]
# The bridge copies rather than aliasing, so a later edit cannot reach back.
source = [[0.1, 0.2]]
bridged = to_channels_first(source)
bridged[0][0] = 9.0
assert source[0][0] == 0.1
try:
    to_channels_first([])
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("empty audio must be refused")

# THE contract that catches everyone: one loader keeps the file exactly as it is...
NATIVE = 48_000
tensor_style = load_contract("torchaudio", NATIVE, 2)
assert tensor_style == {"sample_rate": 48_000, "channels": 2, "ndim": 2}

# ...while the other, by default, silently resamples AND downmixes.
default = load_contract("librosa", NATIVE, 2)
assert default == {"sample_rate": 22_050, "channels": 1, "ndim": 1}, default
assert default["sample_rate"] != NATIVE, "the file's own rate was not preserved"
assert default["channels"] != 2, "the second channel is gone"

# Both defaults are opt-out, and they are separate switches.
assert load_contract("librosa", NATIVE, 2, sr=None)["sample_rate"] == NATIVE
assert load_contract("librosa", NATIVE, 2, sr=None)["channels"] == 1
assert load_contract("librosa", NATIVE, 2, mono=False)["channels"] == 2
assert load_contract("librosa", NATIVE, 2, mono=False)["sample_rate"] == 22_050
faithful = load_contract("librosa", NATIVE, 2, sr=None, mono=False)
assert faithful == {"sample_rate": 48_000, "channels": 2, "ndim": 2}, faithful
assert load_contract("librosa", NATIVE, 2, sr=16_000)["sample_rate"] == 16_000
try:
    load_contract("soundfile", NATIVE, 2)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown library must be refused")

# And the consequence, made concrete: a frame count computed against the assumed
# native rate is simply wrong after a default load.
assumed = frame_count(NATIVE, 512, 256)
resampled_samples = default["sample_rate"]
assert frame_count(resampled_samples, 512, 256) != assumed
assert frame_count(resampled_samples, 512, 256) == 1 + 22_050 // 256

checks.prompt: A training pipeline is slow and occasionally crashes. Profiling shows most time inside per-batch feature extraction using the eager toolkit; the resampling helper is constructed inside the batch loop; and imports fail on one machine after an unrelated framework upgrade. What are the three fixes?
checks.explanation: Three concrete performance and packaging facts. The eager toolkit is single-threaded array code operating on one clip at a time, so per-batch extraction there is a bottleneck by construction — either move it into the batched, accelerator-capable transforms or precompute once. The resampling transform builds a filter kernel when it is constructed, so instantiating it inside a loop repeats that work every call. And the framework-native library is version-locked to the framework itself, so an upgrade of one without the other breaks imports at load time.
options: Move per-batch feature extraction to the framework-native transforms, which batch and run on the accelerator, or precompute features once — the eager toolkit is single-threaded array code and does not belong in a hot loop. Construct the resampler once and reuse it, because it builds a filter kernel on construction. And the framework-native library's version must match the framework's, or imports fail at load
Wrap the eager calls in threads, since the slowness is the interpreter lock; construct the resampler per call to avoid stale state; and pin the operating system's audio codecs
The slowness is the accelerator being idle, fixed by increasing the batch size alone; the resampler is stateless so its construction is free; and import failures indicate a missing audio backend
Precompute nothing and instead lower the number of bands; move resampling to the accelerator without caching; and reinstall the eager toolkit

checks.prompt: Position these two libraries against a general signal-processing package, a plain read-and-write library, and a media conversion tool. Say what each is for. Then advise a team building a music-tagging model: they have a folder of files in assorted formats and sample rates, want to explore which features separate their genres, and will then train a network with augmentation on an accelerator. Describe the pipeline you would recommend, naming which tool does which step and why.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all the tools. The eager array toolkit is for analysis and prototyping on a processor and has the richest set of music features — beat, chroma, onset, pitch — but is eager, single-clip and offers no accelerator or gradients. The framework-native library is for audio as model input: batched, accelerator-ready, differentiable transforms plus datasets and pretrained encoders, at the cost of being tied to its framework and version-locked to it. A general signal-processing package gives low-level filtering, resampling and raw transforms with no audio-specific conveniences, so you assemble the pipeline yourself. A plain read-and-write library handles reading, writing and simple edits but does no feature extraction. A media conversion tool is the universal front door for decoding and converting formats and codecs, and belongs upstream of everything else rather than competing with it. The recommended pipeline must be staged. First, normalise the assorted formats and sample rates with the conversion tool, so everything downstream sees one known rate and channel layout — this also sidesteps the loaders' differing defaults. Second, explore candidate features with the eager toolkit, because its music-analysis toolbox is the reason it exists and exploration is not a hot loop. Third, port the chosen feature computation to the framework-native transforms for training, so extraction is batched, runs on the accelerator and sits inside the graph where augmentation and any learnable front end can be part of the model. A strong answer notes not to compare cepstral feature values across the two libraries because their conventions differ, and warns to pass the explicit arguments that stop the eager loader silently resampling and downmixing during exploration.
